## Design

### 2026-10-18 – I wanted a marble run that keeps going on its own, so the marble has to get back to the top somehow. An Archimedes screw seemed like the neatest way to do that, and I’d never built one, so I spent abo

**5h**

I wanted a marble run that keeps going on its own, so the marble has to get back to the top somehow. An Archimedes screw seemed like the neatest way to do that, and I’d never built one, so I spent about 5 hours on a first model in Fusion.

This was my first time using Fusion, so a big chunk of those hours went on just working out where everything is and how it works: the sketches, the timeline, how to revolve and sweep a shape, how to keep each part as its own body. I spent a lot of time clicking around and undoing things before it started to make sense.

The model had a plinko board, a funnel, a round tube for the track, and the screw sitting inside a closed tube with a small motor on top. Getting it all drawn and lined up took a lot longer than I expected. Every part has to hand the marble to the next one at the right height, and I kept finding that my numbers didn’t add up. The lift wasn’t tall enough for the drop it had to make up.

The screw was the real problem. An 8 mm marble is big next to a 14 mm screw on a 4 mm shaft inside a 16 mm tube, and there’s barely any room for it. I couldn’t see a way to make that work on paper, and once I thought about it properly I didn’t trust it. With the tube closed, if the marble wedges between the flights and the wall, you can’t see it or reach it, and the whole machine just stops. The plinko had the same worry: a marble could get stuck in there with no way to get it out.

So I stopped patching it and started again. The next version has an open channel, a screw with a guide rail and nothing around it, and a plinko tray you can see into. If a marble gets stuck now, I can just see it and flick it out.

### 2026-10-18 – After the first model I started over with one rule: everything has to be open, so I can see the marble the whole way and reach in if it sticks. This took about 8 hours.

**8h**

After the first model I started over with one rule: everything has to be open, so I can see the marble the whole way and reach in if it sticks. This took about 8 hours.

The track. I swapped the closed tube for an open U-shaped channel and made it a lot longer. It now snakes back and forth on two levels (about 770 mm in total) with tight turns at each end, so there’s plenty to watch before the marble gets back to the start.

The screw. I redesigned the Archimedes screw from scratch. It’s now a bigger 20 mm open screw with a thicker 10 mm core, and it leans over a bit, with a vertical guide rail beside it. The marble sits between the screw and the rail, and the rail stops it spinning around with the screw, so the screw pushes it straight up instead. At the top it rolls out over the rail onto a short chute.

Funnel and plinko. I wanted these to be fun to watch, not just there. The chute now drops the marble onto the edge of the funnel, so it circles round and round before it falls through. The plinko is now an open tilted tray with pegs and zig-zag walls, so the marble bounces around on the way down.

Holding it all up. I added slots and posts on the base for the funnel, the plinko and the track, so every part sits in the right place and at the right height. I also drew a box for the control brain and electronics, with a lid, and a hand crank so the screw can be turned by hand without the motor. I printed nothing yet, so all of this is only checked on screen.

Parts. I spent about 40 minutes on Amazon (plus the XIAO board from Seeed) picking the parts: steel balls, an N20 motor, a motor driver, a button, a knob and a USB-C power switch cable. I had to check each one against my design, like the 8 mm ball size and the motor shaft.
